common_name: Flore Pleno Lily of the Valley (True Double-Flowered Lily of the Valley)

planting.note: Plant pips shallowly in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Flore Pleno is the true double-flowered form, distinct from the merely proliferated clusters of 'Prolificans', and increases more slowly than single-flowered cultivars.

directions: Plant pips shallowly in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade. Flore Pleno bears genuinely double, waxy white bells with extra whorls of petals fused into each pendant flower, a rarer and slower-multiplying sport than the branched-stem 'Prolificans' with which it is often confused. It retains the same strong sweet fragrance and paired basal leaves as the species but forms a smaller, tighter colony, making it best suited to a choice spot near a shaded path where the unusual blooms can be admired closely. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from children and pets.

common_name: Golden Jubilee Lily of the Valley (Solid Golden-Leaved Lily of the Valley)

planting.note: Plant pips shallowly in fall or early spring in humus-rich soil in partial shade; Golden Jubilee is a sport of 'Hardwick Hall' with whole leaves in rich golden-yellow rather than a variegated margin, and colors best out of deep shade.

directions: Plant pips shallowly in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade, siting it where morning light or dappled shade can reach the foliage to sustain its color; deep shade fades the leaves toward green. Golden Jubilee arose as a sport of 'Hardwick Hall' but carries solid rich golden-yellow leaves rather than a variegated margin, paired with the same fragrant white bell flowers in spring, and offers a striking foliage accent among green-leaved woodland companions. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from children and pets.

common_name: Bordeaux Lily of the Valley (Large-Flowered Lily of the Valley)

planting.note: Plant pips shallowly in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Bordeaux carries unusually large flowers, 8-12 bells per raceme on tall stems above darker, broader leaves than the species.

directions: Plant pips shallowly in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. Bordeaux is a robust selection prized for its unusually large, intensely fragrant white bells, borne 8 to 12 per raceme on stems held above broad, richly dark green tulip-shaped leaves, a fuller and showier display than the typical species offers. It spreads by rhizome into a dense, vigorous groundcover and tolerates a bit more sun than most cultivars if kept consistently moist. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from children and pets.
